newsitem.title: USA: House committee cuts White House WIC funding request.
newsitem.headline: House committee cuts White House WIC funding request.

text.p: A House panel Wednesday slashed President Clinton's funding request for a special nutrition programme for poor women and children, leading Democrats to warn hundreds of thousands could lose aid.
But Republicans on an appropriations subcommittee charged the Clinton administration padded its spending proposal for the Women, Infants and Children (WIC) nutrition programme.
They said the Agriculture Department already had so much WIC money in reserve it was unlikely anyone would lose benefits.

"There is no diminution of support for this programme," said New York Republican Representative James Walsh. "If there was any serious danger people were going to be taken off the rolls, we would have done more (funding)."
The dispute came as the appropriations subcommittee, which allocates federal funding, worked on an emergency spending bill that will be voted on by the full House later this month.
The subcommittee oversees the WIC programme, providing food vouchers for poor pregnant women and children. The vouchers can be used for baby formula, cereal and other foods.
Currently, 7.4 million people receive benefits under WIC, which has long enjoyed strong bipartisan support.
The Clinton administration wanted Congress to provide an extra $100 million in WIC money through Sept. 30.
That request was based on new state data outlining expected caseloads. The Agriculture Department said without more money, states would have to cut more than 350,000 people off the rolls.
In subcommittee, Democrats offered to accept $76 million. The Republican-led panel on a party-line vote allocated $38 million instead.
"What we're going to do is see several hundred thousand kids go off the programme ... and God help us," said Connecticut Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro.

Wisconsin Democratic Representative David Obey said Congress should err on the side of providing too much, rather than too little, money for the programme. Estimates were that about 180,000 people could lose aid under the lower spending figure.
Agriculture Department press secretary Tom Amontree said the administraiton would "vigorously oppose" the subcommittee decision.

Republicans said the government had about $100 million in WIC funds in reserve that could cover any shortfall. Democrats argued that due to numerous funding uncertainties and changes in caseload, it was impossible to count on reserve funds.
